prompt:
Local fixture (course titles are omitted):

```
Student        Enrolled   Course
sid name year  sid cid    cid dept
 1  Ada   2     1  DB     DB  CS
 2  Ben   1     1  OS     OS  CS
 3  Cat   2     1  LA     LA  MA
 4  Dev   3     2  DB
                3  DB
                3  OS
```

Student has four rows, Enrolled six and Course three. Dev has no enrolment. The attributes are student id `sid`, student `name`, study `year`, course code `cid`, and department `dept`.

how many relational tuples are in the Cartesian product Student × Course (every student paired with every course)?

options.explanation: Correct. Each of the 4 students is paired with each of the 3 courses: 4 × 3 = 12.
That adds the cardinalities (4 + 3). A product pairs every relational tuple with every relational tuple, so it multiplies.
That is the size of Enrolled. A product ignores which pairs are actually enrolled.
That would be a join that keeps one match per student. A product keeps all combinations.

workedExample:
```formula
|R × S| = |R| × |S|
|Student × Course| = 4 × 3 = 12
where
R, S: any two relations
× (between relations): Cartesian product: one relational tuple for every pairing of a relational tuple of R with a relational tuple of S
× (between numbers): multiplication
| |: cardinality: the number of relational tuples in the relation inside the bars
Student: 4 relational tuples (Ada, Ben, Cat, Dev)
Course: 3 relational tuples (DB, course labelled OS, LA)
In words: every one of 4 students is paired with every one of 3 courses, giving 12 relational tuples.
```

The degree (number of attributes) adds instead: Student has 3 attributes and Course 3 (cid, title, dept), so the product has 6.


Student has four rows, Enrolled six and Course three. Dev has no enrolment. The attributes are student id `sid`, student `name`, study `year`, course code `cid`, and department `dept`.

Student has attributes (sid, name, year) and Course has (cid, title, dept). What is the cardinality (number of relational tuples) of the natural join Student ⋈ Course? (⋈ with no condition is the natural join: it matches relational tuples on every attribute name the two relations share.)

options.explanation: A natural join with no shared attributes has no equality conditions to fail, so nothing is filtered out.
There is no join condition to pair each student with a single course.

options.text: It is undefined; natural join requires a common attribute
options.explanation: It is defined. An empty set of join attributes simply gives the product.

options.text: 12, because a natural join on no common attributes is the Cartesian product
options.explanation: Correct. The natural join is the equijoin on all shared attribute names. With none, the condition is empty (always true), so every pair survives: 4 × 3 = 12.

workedExample:
1. Natural join = equijoin on every attribute name the two headings share, keeping one copy of each.
2. Shared names between {sid, name, year} and {cid, title, dept}: **none**.
3. The join condition is the empty conjunction (an "and" of no conditions), which is true for every pair.

```formula
Student ⋈ Course = Student × Course
|Student × Course| = 4 × 3 = 12
where
⋈: natural join: match on all shared attribute names (here there are none)
× (between relations): Cartesian product: every pairing of a student with a course
× (between numbers): multiplication
| |: the number of relational tuples
Student, Course: the lesson's relations, with 4 and 3 relational tuples
In words: with nothing to match on, nothing is filtered out, so the join is the full product: 12 relational tuples.
```

This is also why natural join is dangerous in SQL: renaming or adding a column can silently change what it joins on.


Student has four rows, Enrolled six and Course three. Dev has no enrolment. The attributes are student id `sid`, student `name`, study `year`, course code `cid`, and department `dept`.

how many rows does this query return?

```sql
SELECT *
FROM student s
LEFT JOIN enrolled e
  ON s.sid = e.sid;
```

options.explanation: That is the inner join count. A left outer join also keeps students with no match.
Correct. 6 matched rows from the inner join, plus 1 row for Dev, who has no enrolments, padded with NULLs.
A left join does not reduce to one row per student; a student with three enrolments produces three rows.
That is Student × Enrolled (4 × 6). The ON condition filters the product down.

workedExample:
1. Inner join first: Ada 3 rows, Ben 1, Cat 2, so 6.
2. Students with no match: Dev (sid 4).
3. A left outer join keeps the inner-join rows plus each unmatched left relational tuple, padded with NULL:

```formula
|Student ⟕ Enrolled| = 6 + 1 = 7
where
⟕: left outer join (SQL's LEFT JOIN): the inner join plus every relational tuple of the left input with no partner, padded with NULL
Student, Enrolled: the local student and enrolment relations
| |: the number of rows in the enclosed relation
In words: 6 matched rows plus 1 padded row for Dev gives 7 rows.
```
